sections.html:
Norfolk divides property tax between three bodies. The City Assessor puts a value on your house. The Treasurer prints the bills and takes payment. City Council picks the rate and the due dates each spring with the budget, which means the rate on your own bill is the number to use when you estimate what you owe at a sale.

The city's year runs July 1 through June 30. Every quarter the Treasurer sends statements for over 68,000 taxable parcels, mailing them a month or more ahead of the deadline. Nuisance abatement liens, such as charges for cutting an overgrown lot, are forwarded from Neighborhood Quality to the Treasurer and carry a 30 day payment window.

Four payments a year means a mid-year seller may be closing within weeks of an installment. Plan the closing date around these.

QuarterPeriod coveredDue date
1stJuly 1 to September 30September 30
2ndOctober 1 to December 31December 5
3rdJanuary 1 to March 31March 31
4thApril 1 to June 30June 5

Council can move a date in any given year. When a deadline is near, the date printed on your newest bill wins.

You can start informally with an appraiser or go straight to a formal Board of Review hearing.

  • Informal conference: phone 757-823-1343 to schedule a visit or call with an appraiser. You can ask once the April notice lands, and the window shuts May 8 (the next business day if that date is on a weekend).
  • Formal filing: get your application to the Board of Review, received or postmarked, by the last business day of May.
  • Paperwork: an original and five complete copy sets, with one application per parcel.
  • Agents: a representative must carry the owner's notarized letter of authorization, on letterhead, dated within the same calendar year.

The hearing gives you five minutes. Your job is to show the value sits above the market or is out of line with similar houses. Under Va. Code 58.1-3379 the assessor is presumed right and you bear the burden. If you submit an appraisal, it has to be prepared for appeal purposes, and the city asks for a July 1 value drawn from the prior year's sales.

Before you file, pull together the evidence a hearing officer can act on: recent sales of comparable houses nearby, photos of defects, and repair bids. Label each page with the parcel number so nothing gets separated in the stack of copies.

Miss the May cutoff and the assessor may still listen, but the Board waits until the next year.

The Elizabeth River meets the Chesapeake Bay here, and the city is mostly low ground: roughly 53.28 of its 96.41 square miles are land, at an elevation near 6.9 feet. The 2020 population was 238,005.

Tidal flooding days climbed from about five in 2000 to somewhere around 10 to 15 by 2020, and the 2003 storm surge from Hurricane Isabel reached the Midtown Tunnel. Any seller with an elevation certificate or a flood zone letter in the file should hand it over early. Buyers ask about water almost immediately, and an answer on paper saves a round of back and forth before the contract is signed.

A buyer's insurance bill depends heavily on the flood zone, which is why the city offers a property lookup. Zones come from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map, and the city applies them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The Forerunner site shows flood data for an address and any elevation certificates on record.

  • X: outside the 0.2 percent annual chance of flooding.
  • Shaded X: 0.2 percent annual chance, with depths under 1 foot in a 1 percent event.
  • AE, AH and AO: 1 percent annual chance areas, with AE carrying a mapped base flood elevation.
  • VE and LiMWA: coastal areas affected by wave action.

A house in an AE zone will prompt flood coverage questions from the lender. Regardless of zone, the tax lien still has to be cleared before title passes.

The market spans older waterfront blocks and newly revived districts. Ghent, Colonial Place, Larchmont, North Shore, Edgewater and Lafayette Shores are well known residential pockets, Freemason is the historic district, and Berkley, Willoughby Spit and Ocean View have deep ties to the shoreline.

With Naval Station Norfolk, the largest naval installation in the world, in town, plenty of sellers are service families facing short-notice orders. When there is no time to work through a repair list, selling as is can fit that schedule.

sections.h2: If you sell with tax unpaid
sections.html:
Virginia ranks the real estate tax lien above all others, so a balance gets paid out of your proceeds before you see a check. Va. Code 58.1-3340 tells the purchaser, or the trustee after a foreclosure, to apply the money to taxes and levies on the property, penalties and interest included. After payment the treasurer releases the lien.

How the current period is divided is a contract question, so the purchase agreement should name who covers the open quarter. A grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 under Va. Code 58.1-802 falls on the seller unless the deal says otherwise. The circuit court clerk takes it at recording and splits it between the state and the city.

Letting a bill sit has a worst case. The Treasurer sells parcels with unpaid real estate tax at online-only public auctions under Va. Code 58.1-3975, as is, with a 15 percent buyer's premium.

Get the actual figure first. A payoff from the Treasurer is more reliable than the math on an old bill.

  • Use the eBilling portal or phone the Treasurer to see which quarters remain open.
  • If the value looks too high, call the Assessor at 757-664-4732 and ask how it was set.
  • For possible real estate tax relief, phone the Department of Human Services at 757-823-1130.
  • Mention any nuisance abatement lien to the title company, because the Treasurer collects those as well.

If you want to skip repairs and showings, we can make a written cash offer on a Norfolk house as is, and the title company pays the tax from the proceeds.

Line up the sale timeline with these dates. A listing that starts in late summer can close right as the September 30 installment arrives, while one that closes in May may leave the June 5 bill to sort out.

faqs.q: When is Norfolk real estate tax due?
faqs.a: Four times a year: September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. Bills go out at least a month earlier. Because Council sets the dates and rates annually, rely on the date printed on your current bill.

faqs.q: Who handles questions about my Norfolk assessment?
faqs.a: The City Assessor's office answers value questions at 757-664-4732. For an informal appeal with an appraiser, phone 757-823-1343 once the April notice arrives.

faqs.q: What is the Norfolk Board of Review deadline?
faqs.a: The last business day in May. Submit one application per parcel, with an original and five copies.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Norfolk house if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is deducted from your proceeds at closing and the treasurer releases the lien. Get a payoff figure before you sign a contract.

faqs.q: Does Norfolk auction homes for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer runs online-only public auctions of parcels with unpaid real estate tax under Va. Code 58.1-3975. A sale you arrange yourself keeps price and timing in your hands.
